title: The Ocean Sound That Terrified Scientists

basis.note: median of recent videos; learning gated until day 5

segments.narration: In 1997, oceanic sensors caught an ultra-deep sound booming across the Pacific, louder than any biological creature known to science.
It echoed over three thousand miles. Sci-fi fans panicked, convinced a terrifying sea monster was lurking five miles beneath the surface.
So what made a noise that put blue whales to shame?
In 2012, NOAA scientists analyzed polar recordings and matched the exact acoustic signature. It came from an icequake.
The legendary ocean monster was actually a colossal iceberg cracking off Antarctica.

verdicts.claim: In 1997, underwater hydrophones in the Pacific recorded an extremely loud low-frequency acoustic signal.
verdicts.note: The reference states that Bloop was an ultra-low frequency, high-amplitude underwater sound detected in 1997 by the Equatorial Pacific Ocean hydrophone array.

verdicts.claim: The sound was picked up by sensors spaced over 3,000 miles apart.
verdicts.note: The article explicitly mentions that the sound was detected by sensors up to 4,800 km (3,000 miles) apart.

verdicts.claim: The Bloop sound was significantly louder than a blue whale's vocalization.
verdicts.note: The article notes that the Bloop was 'far louder than any whale noise, or any other animal noise for that matter.'

verdicts.claim: In 2012, NOAA officially identified the sound as an icequake by comparing its acoustic spectrum to polar ice recordings.
verdicts.note: The text states that by 2012, NOAA attributed the sound to a cryoseism (icequake) after finding that numerous icequakes, such as tracking iceberg A53a, shared similar spectrograms with the Bloop.

verdicts.claim: The noise was generated by massive icebergs cracking and breaking away from Antarctic glaciers.
verdicts.note: The text attributes the sound to ice calving and icequakes from glacial movements, with the icebergs involved located near Antarctic regions (Bransfield Strait, Ross Sea, Cape Adare).
